solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Sharp detectives in top case’s start

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is enclosed by it
the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one letter is kept

blocks.note: top-quality is A1, written here as the letters A and I
the Criminal Investigation Department, Britain's plain-clothes police detectives
the opening letter of case

explanation.surface: Keen police detectives are working on the opening of a big case.
explanation.walkthrough: Top-quality is A1, and the digit 1 is read as the letter I. 'Sharp' looks like praise for the detectives but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharp taste is a sour, tangy one, which is what an acid flavour gives, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Concise, really, if somewhat pithy, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives up only its first letter

blocks.note: the first letters of these five words

explanation.surface: Someone praises writing that is brief and, at least somewhat, full of meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition word also supplies the first letter, so the whole clue does double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Crisp prose is brisk and to the point, with no wasted words, which is exactly what concise describes.

indicators.note: oddly points to the odd-numbered positions, so the first and third letters are kept
taking something in means holding it inside, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: an illness is a disease
the first and third letters of pill

explanation.surface: A patient makes their sickness worse by swallowing the wrong tablet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aggravate' in the surface means make worse, but here it has its informal sense of annoy.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal use to aggravate someone is to irritate or annoy them, the same as to displease.

clue.text: Pirates with origin of cross bones

indicators.note: the origin of a word is where it begins, its first letter

blocks.note: the first letter of cross
ribs are bones of the chest

explanation.surface: Pirates sail under the skull and crossbones flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pirates' is a verb, not the sailors of the surface: to pirate is to copy without permission.
explanation.definitionFit: To crib is to copy someone else's work dishonestly, and to pirate is likewise to copy illicitly.

indicators.note: banks are the edges of a river, so only the outer letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of study
a stem is a branch of a plant, or a line of descent

explanation.surface: Bank managers set out to examine how their branch network is organised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' reads as financial institutions, but it means the edges of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A system is an organised arrangement of connected parts, which is one sense of a structure.

clue.text: Upset American who’s buying underwear item?

indicators.note: in a down clue something upset is turned upside down, so its letters run the other way

blocks.note: US is short for American
someone buying things is a spender

explanation.surface: A disgruntled American shopper is in the lingerie department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' seems to describe the American's mood, but it turns US over.
explanation.definitionFit: A suspender is an elastic strap worn to hold up stockings or socks, an item of underwear.

clue.text: Rocked for the audience in leather

indicators.note: an audience listens, so the word is to be judged by its sound

blocks.note: rocked means moved from side to side

explanation.surface: A performer in leather gear rocks out for the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocked' suggests rock music, but it means moved to and fro.
explanation.definitionFit: Suede is leather with the flesh side rubbed to a soft napped finish, so it is a kind of leather.

indicators.note: a phrase that includes something holds it within its own run of letters

blocks.note: the letters run on across the three words

explanation.surface: Someone complains that it is unwise to put a train journey on the schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' sounds like a railway service, but it is the followers trailing behind someone important.
explanation.definitionFit: A train is a retinue of attendants following a dignitary, which is what an entourage is.

indicators.note: one thing lying over another covers it all round, so it wraps the rest

blocks.note: a tiff is a minor quarrel
taken as written
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A political row breaks out over a tax brought in by a Republican.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'over' as about; in the wordplay the quarrel goes round A and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A tariff is a duty charged on imported or exported goods, a particular kind of tax.

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading from bottom to top, the opposite way

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
to scoff is to mock or sneer

explanation.surface: A child is told to be good and wolf down their vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoff' in the surface means eat greedily, but in the wordplay it means jeer.
explanation.definitionFit: Greens are leafy green vegetables such as cabbage and kale, and veggies is informal for vegetables.

blocks.note: surface reading: the South American country is remarkably lengthy, as it famously is
setter's reading: the farewell that a Spanish speaker in Chile would say

explanation.walkthrough: Chile really is a very long, thin country, so the clue seems to marvel at its length; 'so long' is in fact a goodbye, said in Spanish.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish word is the ordinary farewell in Chile, equivalent to English goodbye or cheerio.

clue.text: One studies bug, otherwise keeping quiet

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: a bug is an insect
P is piano, the musical instruction to play quietly
or introduces an alternative, as otherwise does

explanation.surface: An entomologist examines an insect, or else keeps silent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' suggests a hidden microphone, fitting the investigator, but it is simply an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: An inspector is someone whose job is to examine things closely, a person who studies or scrutinises.

clue.text: Spikes demon drink with soda, principally

indicators.note: principally means first and foremost, so only the leading letter is kept

blocks.note: an imp is a small demon
ale is a drink
the first letter of soda

explanation.surface: Someone laces a fiendish drink, mostly with soda water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spikes' looks like doctoring a drink, but it is a verb meaning pierces with a point.
explanation.definitionFit: To spike is to pierce with a sharp point, which is what impaling does to its victim.

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
the central letter of sweet, its heart
sweet in the sense of charming or endearing

explanation.surface: A performer is delighted to share the stage with an old flame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweetheart' splits into former, then the heart of sweet; the final exclamation is a separate synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To execute a manoeuvre or a plan is to carry it out, the same as to perform it.

indicators.note: to assume something is to take it on, so one piece takes another inside it

blocks.note: to ford a river is to wade across it
war is armed battle

explanation.surface: An army wades across a river, expecting a fight, and pushes on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assuming' reads as supposing in the surface, but here it means taking on.
explanation.definitionFit: To forward something is to promote or help it along, so forwarded and advanced are synonyms.

clue.text: Support control in favour of Church

blocks.note: to rein in is to control, as with a horse
to be for something is to favour it
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Backing for tighter control is expressed by those who favour the Church.
explanation.walkthrough: CE, the Church of England, is a common crossword abbreviation for church.
explanation.definitionFit: To reinforce a wall or an argument is to strengthen or prop it up, which is to support it.

clue.text: On record, detectives essentially censure protester

indicators.note: the essence of something is at its core, so only the central letter is kept

blocks.note: DIs are detective inspectors
the central letter of the seven in censure
to enter something is to put it on record

explanation.surface: Police, speaking officially, fundamentally condemn a demonstrator.
explanation.walkthrough: The first words are placed last: 'On record' is read as the verb enter, as in entering a figure in a ledger.
explanation.definitionFit: A dissenter disagrees with established views and objects openly, so they are a kind of protester.

clue.text: Men in leather trousers displaying rear

blocks.note: first meaning: fellows, blokes
second meaning: cowboys' leather leggings, open at the back

explanation.surface: Some men in bottomless leather trousers put on a cheeky display.
explanation.walkthrough: Chaps are worn over ordinary trousers, joined only at the waist, so they leave the seat uncovered, which the second definition describes.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is British informal for men or fellows, and also names the leather leg coverings worn by cowboys.

indicators.note: to captivate is literally to take captive, so one piece is imprisoned inside another

blocks.note: a con is a convict, and with the apostrophe s it becomes con's
a yarn is a story or tale
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A crook's story wins over a British policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: A bobby is British slang for a police officer, named after Sir Robert Peel, who founded the Metropolitan Police.
explanation.definitionFit: A constable is a police officer of the lowest rank, the ordinary bobby on the beat.

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
seasoned means matured, and ripe fruit or cheese is matured

explanation.surface: Garden rhubarb matures only with the passing of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rhubarb' looks like the vegetable, but it is British slang for nonsense. 'By' puts time beside the other piece, here in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are British informal terms for nonsense or rubbish, especially talk that is worthless.

indicators.note: to turn out is to eject what is inside, leaving only the outside letters

blocks.note: the first and last letters of tough
to rob is to steal

explanation.surface: A man who grew up to be a thug is stealing money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pounds' suggests sterling cash for the thief, but it is a verb, beats heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: A heart or a headache that pounds beats with strong rhythmic pulses, which is to throb.

clue.text: Demanding part of cost ring entailed

indicators.note: only a part of the phrase is wanted, a run of letters inside it

blocks.note: the letters run on across the three words

explanation.surface: Some of the expense of a price-fixing cartel was a heavy burden.
explanation.walkthrough: A ring here is a cartel of dealers fixing prices, which sets the surface's scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Stringent rules are strict and exacting, making heavy demands on those who must follow them.

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so its letters run the other way
one thing about another goes around it, enclosing it

blocks.note: a tart remark is sharp and cutting
e.g. means for example, that is, say

explanation.surface: Someone is scornful of, for example, a wretched cigarette end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swear word and 'butt' like a cigarette end; really the butt is someone at the receiving end of jokes.
explanation.definitionFit: The butt of jokes or criticism is the person aimed at, so butt and target are synonyms.

clue.text: Concerned with release involving English judge

indicators.note: to involve is to wrap in, so one piece contains another

blocks.note: re means concerning, as in business letters
to release is to set free
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A case about freeing someone comes before an English judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' suggests a courtroom, but it is the official who adjudicates a game.
explanation.definitionFit: A referee rules on disputes in a sporting match and can be called on to arbitrate, so a judge.

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: the last letter of watercolour
oils are oil paints

explanation.surface: An artist spoils a watercolour at the end by adding oil paint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muddies' is a verb here, matching the answer ending in S.
explanation.definitionFit: To roil water is to stir up its sediment and make it cloudy, which is to muddy it.

blocks.note: first meaning: comparative of butch, tougher and more manly
second meaning: a tradesperson who sells meat

explanation.surface: A beefy man is asked who is the manlier of the two.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the answer as butch plus the comparative ending -er, which is why it is more masculine.
explanation.definitionFit: Butch means tough and macho, so its comparative fits the first; a meat trader supplies beef, so it fits the second.

indicators.note: to embody is to hold within one's body, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a bust is a sculpture of head and shoulders
R stands for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: Someone smashes a statue portraying the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: R, for Regina, is a standard crossword abbreviation for queen.
explanation.definitionFit: To burst is to break apart suddenly and violently, a close synonym of shatter.

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: hoar means greyish-white, as in hoar frost
the last letter of furred

explanation.surface: A grey squirrel ends up with a thick coat of fur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squirrel' is the verb, as in squirrel away, not the grey animal of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To squirrel things away is to store them up secretly for later, which is what hoarding means.

clue.text: Brief obstruction if stone gets lodged

indicators.note: something lodged is stuck fast inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: a barrier is an obstruction
ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight of 14 pounds

explanation.surface: A short blockage occurs when a stone gets stuck, as in a kidney or a pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like an adjective for the obstruction; it is the noun, British slang for a lawyer, who receives a brief.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a brief is a lawyer, especially a barrister, who argues cases in the higher courts.

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

explanation.surface: Soldiers in barracks now and then show some self-control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barrack' can be a noun, the soldiers' quarters, or a British verb meaning to jeer; neither sense matters, since only its letters count.
explanation.definitionFit: A brake is anything that checks or slows progress, so used figuratively it is a restraint.

clue.text: More abrupt language in discontented temper

indicators.note: without its contents a word keeps only its outer letters
one thing in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: the first and last letters of temper
Erse is the Gaelic language of Scotland or Ireland

explanation.surface: Someone speaks more curtly when in a bad mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discontented' reads as unhappy, fitting the bad temper, but it means with the contents removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Terse means brief and curt in speech, so the comparative matches more abrupt, short to the point of rudeness.

indicators.note: one thing around another encircles it, so it holds the other inside

blocks.note: to have a shot is to have a try
an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: A football shot curling around the goalkeeper ends up in the net.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' seems to say the shot went in; it is the definition, meaning fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is in is currently fashionable, and trendy means following the latest fashion.
